tasks.title: Predict How Filters Handle Null Readings

description.context: Spark uses SQL three-valued logic: every comparison returns TRUE, FALSE, or NULL. When a column is null, ANY comparison on it (>, <, ==, !=) evaluates to NULL — not FALSE. filter() keeps rows where the condition is TRUE and DISCARDS rows where it is FALSE OR NULL. This means filter(col('x') > 0) does NOT just discard rows where x <= 0; it also discards rows where x is null. The same applies to the NEGATED filter — filter(~(col('x') > 0)) discards null rows too, because NOT NULL is still NULL. So filter(C) and filter(~C) together do NOT cover the whole table — null rows are missing from BOTH results.
description.task: Predict the row count for each filter and explain why the parts do not sum to the whole.
description.validationHint: Remember: when daily_kw is null, any comparison (>, <, ==, !=) evaluates to null, and filter() discards null results along with false results.

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: df has 121 rows total. Distribution of daily_kw: 8 null, 5 negative, 2 zero, 106 positive.

evidence.label: Three filter expressions
evidence.content:
result_a = df.filter(col('daily_kw') > 0)
result_b = df.filter(col('daily_kw') >= 0)
result_c = df.filter(~(col('daily_kw') > 0))

fields.label: How many rows does result_a contain? (filter: daily_kw > 0)
fields.rationale: daily_kw > 0 keeps the 106 positive rows. Nulls are discarded (null > 0 → null → discarded). Negatives are discarded (negative > 0 → false). Zeros are discarded (0 > 0 → false).

fields.label: How many rows does result_b contain? (filter: daily_kw >= 0)
fields.rationale: daily_kw >= 0 keeps the 106 positive rows plus 2 zero-value rows (0 >= 0 → true). Nulls are discarded. Negatives are discarded.

fields.label: How many rows does result_c contain? (filter: NOT daily_kw > 0)
fields.rationale: ~(col('daily_kw') > 0) inverts the boolean. For positive values: NOT true → false → discarded. For negatives: NOT false → true → kept (5 rows). For zeros: NOT false → true → kept (2 rows). For nulls: NOT null → null → discarded. Total: 5 + 2 = 7. The trap: students might expect 121 - 106 = 15, but nulls are discarded by both the original and the negated filter.

fields.label: Why don't result_a and result_c add up to 121 (the total rows)?
options: Because filter() has a rounding error when counting rows; row counts in Spark are approximations.

Because null rows are discarded by BOTH filters — null > 0 evaluates to null, NOT(null > 0) also evaluates to null, and filter discards null in both cases. The 8 null rows are missing from both results.
Because zero-value rows are counted in both results, double-counting them and inflating the sum above 121.
Because Spark automatically deduplicates rows when applying NOT-style filters, so duplicates collapse to a single row.
fields.correctAnswer: Because null rows are discarded by BOTH filters — null > 0 evaluates to null, NOT(null > 0) also evaluates to null, and filter discards null in both cases. The 8 null rows are missing from both results.
fields.rationale: Three-valued logic in SQL/Spark: NULL is not FALSE. NOT(NULL) is still NULL. So filter(C) and filter(~C) both discard the same null rows, not partition them. Sum: 106 + 7 = 113, exactly 121 - 8 (the null count). The most common Junior confusion is treating null as 'just another value' or as 'falsy'; in Spark null is genuinely a third truth value with its own propagation rules.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Spark counts are exact, not approximate.

Option C: Zeros are not in either result for filter > 0 (false), so cannot inflate.

Option D: Filter does not deduplicate; that is dropDuplicates' job.

description.context: Four PySpark conventions trip up Juniors. (1) drop() is FORGIVING — passing a non-existent column name is silent no-op (no error), unlike select() which DOES error. (2) filter() and where() are LITERAL ALIASES — same method under the hood, identical behavior, identical performance. (3) Catalyst FUSES chained filters into one compound predicate; df.filter(A).filter(B).filter(C) plans the same as df.filter(A & B & C). (4) Python's `&` operator has LOWER precedence than `>` and `==` — meaning col('x') > 0 & col('y') == 'NORTH' parses as col('x') > (0 & col('y')) == 'NORTH', which is a type error. The fix is parens around each comparison: (col('x') > 0) & (col('y') == 'NORTH').
description.task: Predict the behavior of each snippet.
description.validationHint: Remember that filter() and where() are aliases, chained filters are fused by Catalyst, and drop() silently ignores missing columns.

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Four code snippets from a code review; predict what each does.

fields.label: Code: df.drop('nonexistent_column') — what happens?
options: Spark raises an AnalysisException because the column does not exist; you must check df.columns first.
Spark silently returns the DataFrame unchanged — drop() is forgiving on missing columns and only removes columns that actually exist.
Spark removes all columns and returns an empty DataFrame, on the theory that 'nonexistent' matches nothing so everything is dropped by default.
Spark removes the first column as a fallback when the named column cannot be found.
fields.correctAnswer: Spark silently returns the DataFrame unchanged — drop() is forgiving on missing columns and only removes columns that actually exist.
fields.rationale: drop() is intentionally forgiving — it is meant to be safe to call defensively (e.g., drop('temp_col') in cleanup code that may or may not have created the column). select() is strict because it is asking for specific columns to keep, where missing names indicate a bug. The most common Junior confusion is expecting symmetric behavior between select and drop; in fact they are deliberately asymmetric.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: drop() does not error on missing columns; that is select()'s behavior.

Option C: drop with a name that does not exist removes nothing.

Option D: No fallback exists; missing names are simply ignored.

fields.label: Are df.filter(col('daily_kw') > 0) and df.where(col('daily_kw') > 0) functionally different?
options: Yes — filter() is faster because it was implemented first and has more Catalyst optimizations.
Yes — where() checks for nulls automatically while filter() does not, so they produce different row counts on null-bearing columns.
No — where() is a literal alias for filter() in PySpark; they call the same Java method and produce identical plans.
No — they produce the same result but where() skips Catalyst optimization to feel more SQL-like.
fields.correctAnswer: No — where() is a literal alias for filter() in PySpark; they call the same Java method and produce identical plans.
fields.rationale: filter and where are aliases — pick whichever reads better in context. They share an implementation, a plan, and performance characteristics. The most common Junior confusion is treating method-name diversity as feature diversity; in PySpark several methods are aliases for SQL/Pandas familiarity (drop_duplicates / dropDuplicates is another).
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Performance is identical because the implementation is identical.

Option B: Both filter and where treat null comparisons identically.

Option D: Optimization runs the same way for both.

fields.label: A pipeline chains 5 filter() calls: df.filter(A).filter(B).filter(C).filter(D).filter(E). Does Spark scan the data 5 times?
options: Yes — each .filter() returns a new DataFrame and each new DataFrame triggers its own data scan.
No — Catalyst FUSES adjacent filters into a single compound predicate (A & B & C & D & E) so the data is scanned once when an action triggers.
No — Spark only executes the LAST filter and ignores the first four; this is why chaining filters is anti-pattern.
It depends on whether the filters use & inside one filter() vs being chained separately; chained ones are slow.
fields.correctAnswer: No — Catalyst FUSES adjacent filters into a single compound predicate (A & B & C & D & E) so the data is scanned once when an action triggers.
fields.rationale: The optimizer collapses chained filters into one. The chained style is purely a readability choice. The most common Junior confusion is fearing that chaining costs performance; in reality the compound and chained styles produce identical plans, so engineers should pick whichever is more readable.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Lazy evaluation means filters do not execute until an action; chaining adds plan nodes, not scans.

Option C: All filters apply; none are dropped.

Option D: Compound and chained styles plan identically.

fields.label: The engineer writes: df.filter(col('daily_kw') > 0 & col('region') == 'NORTH'). What happens?
options: It correctly filters for positive readings in the NORTH region by combining both conditions with &.
It raises a TypeError or AnalysisException because Python's & binds tighter than > and ==, parsing as col('daily_kw') > (0 & col('region')) == 'NORTH'; you must wrap each comparison in parentheses.
It filters for NORTH only because Python evaluates the right side of & first and ignores the left.
It filters for positive daily_kw only because Python short-circuits & when the left side is true.
fields.correctAnswer: It raises a TypeError or AnalysisException because Python's & binds tighter than > and ==, parsing as col('daily_kw') > (0 & col('region')) == 'NORTH'; you must wrap each comparison in parentheses.
fields.rationale: Python operator precedence puts & ABOVE > and ==. So Spark sees `0 & col('region')` first, which is bitwise-AND of an int and a Column — type error. The fix: (col('daily_kw') > 0) & (col('region') == 'NORTH'). The most common Junior confusion is assuming & follows English logic ('and is between A and B'); in Python, & is a bitwise/boolean operator with high precedence.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Without parens, the expression does not parse as intended.

Option C: Python does not short-circuit & in the way described.

Option D: Same — no short-circuiting, just precedence error.

tasks.title: Build NordGrid's Complete Bronze-to-Silver Pipeline

description.context: NordGrid's data engineering team needs a complete Bronze-to-Silver pipeline for the daily meter readings. The pipeline must handle every data quality issue present in the Bronze dataset: null readings, negative sensor errors, duplicate ingestion batches, and extra metadata columns. The Silver output must have exactly four columns named meter_id, energy_kw, reading_date, and region.
description.task: Write a chained transformation pipeline that: (1) reads PS4_data_readings.csv with header and inferSchema; (2) filters out null daily_kw values; (3) filters out negative daily_kw values but keeps zeros; (4) removes duplicate rows based on meter_id and date; (5) produces the final output with exactly four columns — meter_id, daily_kw aliased as energy_kw, date aliased as reading_date, and region. Use the parenthesized chaining style. Store the result in a variable called silver.
description.validationHint: Start with 121 rows. Remove 8 nulls (→ 113). Remove 5 negatives (→ 108). Remove 6 duplicates (→ 102). Final schema: 4 columns. The order of dedup vs filter may slightly change the count if duplicates have null/negative values — apply filters first, then dedup.

tasks.partialCredit: 7 independent assertions. Each passed assertion earns 1/7 credit.

conceptsCombined: select() with alias() for column shaping and renaming (Lessons 1, 8)
Chained filter() calls for null and negative removal (Lessons 4-6)
dropDuplicates() on key columns for dedup (Lesson 9)
synthesisNotes.rationale: This task is the full Bronze-to-Silver pipeline that Module 4 builds toward. The student must combine column shaping, null handling, negative filtering with zero preservation, deduplication, and renaming in a single chained pipeline. The order matters: filtering before dedup is the correct pattern because it removes invalid rows before dedup considers key uniqueness.
